haiku-low.q1: On-call runs the failover command by hand after confirming A is lost. Detection alone never fails over; it only pages on-call.
haiku-low.q2: The command stops and prints the reason before anything changes. It continues only with the explicit accept-data-loss override, which is logged.
haiku-low.q3: Promotion: fence wait elapsed. Workers: promotion confirmed and jobs requeued. DNS: 12 healthy B instances and B /healthz passing.
haiku-low.q4: Users must sign in again after traffic moves to B.
haiku-low.q5: A is queued for rebuild as a replica of B. It stays fenced and is never reused as primary until rebuilt; failback is a separate planned switchover.
haiku-low.q6: Lease fencing: the store refuses A's renewals after the flip, so A's watchdog stops Postgres and blocks port 5432 within 15 s.
haiku-low.q7: A small three-member consensus store (e.g., etcd) holds it. Read by A's DB watchdog, both /healthz, job workers, and the failover command; written by the failover command and A's lease renewals.
haiku-low.q8: Running rows with claim epoch below n+1 go to queued with attempt+1, or to needs_review if the job type is not safe to rerun.
haiku-low.q9: Rerun the command; done steps are skipped and a stale lock is taken over. Going back to A is possible only before the flip.
haiku-low.q10: Cached DNS keeps the client on A until the TTL expires, about 60 s after the DNS change, then it moves to B.
haiku-low.q11: Up to about 30 s of committed data (RPO 30 s). Limited by the replay-lag check (30 s) and the renewal check (15 s after B's last WAL receipt).

sonnet.q1: A failover is started only by on-call running the failover command by hand, after confirming A is lost. Detection (probes: 2 of 3 locations see 3 consecutive failures of /healthz) only pages on-call; it never fails over by itself.
sonnet.q2: The loss pre-check fails (B's last recorded replay lag over 30 s, or A's last lease renewal more than 15 s after B's last WAL receipt). The command stops before anything changes and A stays active. It continues only if the explicit accept-data-loss override is given, which is logged in the record.
sonnet.q3: Before B's DB is promoted: the flip is committed (record says B, epoch n+1, FENCING) and the 20 s fence wait has elapsed. Before B's workers start: promotion confirmed (out of recovery, marker row written) and the job requeue done. Before DNS moves: the health gate passes (12 B web instances healthy, and B /healthz passes: DB writable, Redis up, record says B), which waits on the web scale-up and the started workers.
sonnet.q5: It stays fenced. A's Postgres always boots fenced and opens for writes only if the record says A at the current epoch, which it never says again after a failover. It is never reused as primary; A is queued for rebuild as a replica of B.
sonnet.q6: The lease fencing in A. A's DB watchdog must renew a lease every 3 s, and the store accepts renewals only while the record says A, epoch n. After the flip renewals are refused, or a cut-off A cannot reach the store majority. After 15 s with no successful renewal, the watchdog stops Postgres and blocks port 5432 (a kernel watchdog resets the host if the watchdog hangs). The command waits 20 s after the flip before promoting B, so A has stopped writing first.
sonnet.q7: A small consensus store (for example etcd) with three members: one in A, one in B, and a witness in a third location. The failover command writes it (compare-and-set flip, state, DONE). A's watchdog renews its lease there. A's DB watchdog, both regions' /healthz, the job workers, and the failover command read it. DNS does not hold the record.
sonnet.q8: They are rerun. After promotion, the requeue step moves every running row with claim epoch below n+1 to queued with attempt+1, or to needs_review if the job type is not safe to rerun (those are never rerun automatically). External calls carry the job id as idempotency key. B's workers start only after the requeue is confirmed.
sonnet.q9: Run the command again. Every step after the flip checks its done condition and skips itself if done. If the previous run died, its lock heartbeat goes stale after 30 s and the new run takes over. It sees the record already says B, epoch n+1, skips pre-checks, re-waits the full 20 s fence unless B is already writable, resets the web desired count, and continues from the first step not done. Going back to A is only possible before the flip, when nothing has changed and A stays active (fix the cause and rerun). After the flip nothing can be undone and no path unfences A. Failback is a separate planned switchover after A is rebuilt as a replica of B.
sonnet.q10: NOT STATED in detail. The document says only that clients move within about 60 s of TTL after the traffic manager is pointed at B and A is marked disabled. What a client with a stale cached record sees is not described, other than that A's DB is fenced and stopped by then.
sonnet.q11: Up to about 30 s (RPO 30 s). It is limited by two pre-checks: B's last recorded replay lag must be at most 30 s, and A's last lease renewal must be at most 15 s after B's last WAL receipt. The second covers a cut-off A that keeps committing writes B never receives, because A can write at most 15 s past its last renewal. If either fails the command stops, unless the accept-data-loss override is given, and then more can be lost.
